name: Senoufo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Mills, Elizabeth. 1984. Senoufo phonology, discourse to syllable (a prosodic approach). Summer Institute of Linguistics Publications in Linguistics 72. Dallas: Summer Institute of Linguistics and University of Texas at Arlington.
catalog_locator: p. 119, sec. 8.2.2 Stress; supporting p. 107, sec. 7.1
catalog_quote: Stress is a demarcative, nondistinctive feature serving as a cohesive factor within the word and occurring once in each basic word. It is realized as a long and fortis articulation of the onset consonant of the stressed syllable, and as an intense articulation of that syllable. ... Word stress is different from sentence initial stress and focal stress. ... Stress always occurs on the first syllable of the basic word. Closely associated with it are the features of length, secondary release, and long rhythm units, which all occur only word initially in the basic word. ... Stress always follows open juncture: either external word juncture or internal open juncture (page 173). Any word containing more than one stressed syllable is a compound word, and internal open juncture precedes the medial stressed syllable.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had
sweep_summary: Senari (ceba1235) is not in the catalog. Both works with stress in the title are Elizabeth Mills' hierarchical/prosodic phonology of the Tyebaara (Korhogo) dialect. The 1984 SIL PL 72 book was already held by the project (scan, no text) with an scanned of the stress pages from an earlier reading;119, sect. 8.2.2): stress is demarcative and non-distinctive and 'always occurs on the first syllable of the basic word', realized as fortis/long onset consonant plus syllable intensity, never as vowel lengthening; expanded words stress the initial syllable only (p.163), compounds stress each nucleus after internal open juncture with unstressed satellites (pp.171, 173). Preface p.xiii ties the description to central Senari (Tyebaara of Korhogo). The 1978 ILA Abidjan item (Glottolog 105749, xv+264, 'Thesis?') could not be located in any open repository (OpenLibrary, archive.org, Crossref, Bing all empty; HathiTrust/WorldCat/Google Books/sil. the 1984 Acknowledgements (p.xix) show it is the earlier ILA-affiliated version of the same study, so its acquisition priority is low. Best new statement: Mills 1984 p.119 — fixed initial, demarcative word stress in a tone language; no catalog source to supersede. ( updated).

new_statements.quote: 8.2.2 Stress is a demarcative, nondistinctive feature serving as a cohesive factor within the word and occurring once in each basic word. It is realized as a long and fortis articulation of the onset consonant of the stressed syllable, and as an intense articulation of that syllable. [...] Although the consonant is longer in stressed syllables than in unstressed ones, vowels are not lengthened because of word stress. [...] Stress always occurs on the first syllable of the basic word. [...] Stress always follows open juncture: either external word juncture or internal open juncture (page 173). Any word containing more than one stressed syllable is a compound word, and internal open juncture precedes the medial stressed syllable.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (247 pp., image-only scan, extracted text returns nothing; PDF page = book page + 30). I re-rendered pp.149, 150, 193, 203 and 15 (book pp.119, 120, 163, 173, xiii) at 120 dpi and read the page scan directly rather than relying on the compilers scanned file. (1) Verbatim: book p.119, sect. 8.2.2 reads exactly as quoted (with the marked ellipses): 'Stress is a demarcative, nondistinctive feature serving as a cohesive factor within the word and occurring once in each basic word. It is realized as a long and fortis articulation of the onset consonant of the stressed syllable, and as an intense articulation of that syllable.. Although the consonant is longer in stressed syllables…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and demarcative: every basic (monomorphemic) word and every expanded word (stem plus clitics/suffixes) carries a single stress on its first syllable, cued mainly by a long, fortis onset consonant rather than by loudness, pitch or vowel length; lexical tone (five tonemes) is the distinctive prosody. Compound words carry a stress on the initial syllable of each nuclear component, each preceded by (internal) open juncture.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No primary/secondary ranking within the word: in compounds 'the rhythm units preceding and following internal juncture are of equal intensity: both units carry word stress' (p.173); the compound's satellite is unstressed (p.171). 'Secondary paragraph stress' in the book is a discourse-level notion, not word-level.
new_statements.exceptions: Particles/clitics (e.g. TAM markers) are stressed only when they stand word-initially and lose stress when medial in an expanded word (p.120); the syllable after prefinal (semi-open) juncture is never stressed (p.121); borrowed words with non-native shapes are treated like compounds (p.116). Sentence-initial and focal stress (loudness, wide tone intervals, extra duration) are explicitly distinguished from word stress (p.119).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word ('basic word' = one morpheme; 'expanded word' = stress group incl. clitics, initial stress only; 'compound word' = one stress per nuclear component). Description is of connected speech within a discourse-to-syllable prosodic hierarchy, with instrumental duration measurements (centiseconds) supporting the consonant-length correlate.
new_statements.identity_note: Mills 1984 describes "the central Senari (Tyebaara dialect) of Korhogo" (Glottolog's record localizes it to Dokaha-Tiorognadougou just south of Korhogo). Tyebaara/Tyebara/Tiembara/Kiembara is the reference dialect of Cebaara Senoufo [sef], glottocode ceba1235; no separate dialect-level glottocode needed.

new_statements.reading: Senari (Cebaara Senoufo, Tyebaara of Korhogo) has fixed word-initial stress in the basic word; the stress is demarcative and non-contrastive (realized as consonant fortis/length and syllable intensity, not vowel length), while lexical tone is the distinctive prosody. Compounds carry one stress per nucleus (initial syllable of each), satellites are unstressed. Coding candidate: fixed initial stress, demarcative, tone language.

tone_statements.citation: Silué, Songfolo Lacina. 2025. La syntaxe du discours rapporté en kafire (langue sénoufo de Côte d’Ivoire) : une approche lexicale-fonctionnelle. Thèse de doctorat, Institut National des Langues et Civilisations Orientales (INALCO), Paris (soutenue le 23 janvier 2025; NNT 2025INAL0001). 459 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Nous déterminons 5 tonèmes en kafire en l’occurence, les trois tons simples haut, moyen, bas et les deux tons complexes bas-haut et haut-bas. Nous donnons quelques illustrations du rôle discriminatoire des tons simples dans le tableau 1.8. Il s’agit particulièrement de l’opposition du ton haut au ton moyen. ... Le ton montant (=bas-haut) et le ton descendant (=haut-bas) sont des tonèmes dans la langue. ... Notons par contre que le ton bas-haut peut également résulter de la manifestation en surface d’un ton bas qui se réalise tantôt bas, tantôt bas-haut.
tone_statements.translation: We identify 5 tonemes in Kafire, namely the three simple tones high, mid, low and the two complex tones low-high and high-low. We give some illustrations of the distinctive role of the simple tones in table 1.8, in particular the opposition of high tone to mid tone. ... The rising (=low-high) tone and the falling (=high-low) tone are tonemes in the language. ... Note however that the low-high tone can also result from the surface realisation of a low tone, which is realised sometimes low, sometimes low-high.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 25-26, ch. 1, sect. 1.3.3 'Les suprasegments', 1.3.3.1 'Les tonèmes' (tone rules 1.3.3.2, pp. 26-29)
tone_statements.summary: 3 level tones H, M, L + 2 contour tonemes LH, HL (5 tonemes); L -> LH in isolation (floating H after L); L-to-R spreading onto toneless grammatical morphemes; H-H lowering (pronoun H -> L before H verb/postposition).

tone_statements.citation: Diarassouba, Sidiky. 2007. Establishment of Literacy Standards for an Oral Language: The Case of Nafara Discourse Patterns, Cote d'Ivoire, West Africa. PhD dissertation, Florida State University, College of Education (Department of Middle and Secondary Education; directed by Pamela S. Carroll). DigiNole fsu:168913.
tone_statements.quote: Note: The three tones in Nafara will confer a variety of sounds to the same letter. For instance, all vowels and a few consonants, such as m, n and w may take any of the tones, which thus indicate a nuance or totally different semantic field of the morpheme. … However, there are fewer morphological inflections and more phonological changes that mark tenses. In other words, in most cases when changes occur it is about a shift in the tone. We may say Nafara is a tonal language par excellence.
tone_statements.locator: Appendix B, note under Table 1A, p. 295 … 'Morphological Inflections and Phonological Shifts', p. 322
tone_statements.summary: Nafara (Senari) is described as a tone language with three tones that distinguish word meanings and mark tense; the tones are not named or analysed (only 'high tone' and 'low tone' occur in passing).

It is realized as a long and fortis articulation of the onset consonant of the stressed syllable, and as an intense articulation of that syllable. sources.locator: Ch. 8 'The Basic Word', sect. 8.2.2 Stress, book p.119 (p.149); supporting: p.120 (PDF 150), sect. 9.1 p.163 (PDF 193), pp.171,173 (PDF 201,203), Introduction p.xxvii (PDF 29)
sources.note: Sect. 8.2.2 (p.119): word stress is demarcative and non-distinctive, occurs once per basic word, always on the first syllable, realized as long/fortis onset consonant (not vowel length, loudness or pitch); expanded words also initial-only (p.163); compound words carry stress on each nuclear component, of equal intensity, separated by internal open juncture (pp.171,173); clitic particles are stressed only when word-initial (p.120). Tone (5 tonemes) is the distinctive prosody; sentence/paragraph 'stress' (loudness, pitch range) is a separate higher-level phenomenon.
